item.title: What Shapes Independent Political Identity?
item.description:
Identity

What Shapes Independent Political Identity?

Why we should embrace 45 percent of Americans for who they are.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Americans today are far more likely to identify as an Independent than either a Democrat or a Republican.
  • The development of a political identity often precedes the formation of partisan attachments.
  • Independents are motivated by a desire for more authentic forms of political engagement.
  • The future of American democracy depends on engaging Independents as themselves.

According to a 2026 Gallup poll, 45 percent of Americans identify as Independent, while 27 percent identify as Democrats and 27 percent identify as Republicans. The two legacy parties in the United States would have you believe there are only two options for political identity—you’re either a Democrat or a Republican. However, Americans today are far more likely to identify as an Independent than either a Democrat or a Republican.

This trend has been well researched since at least the 1960s. Between the 1960 and 2012 elections, the share of self-identified Independents doubled from 23 percent to 46 percent, rendering Independents the most populous category of self-identification in 2012. If this trend continues, those with Independent political identity may soon be in the majority in the United States. So, perhaps we should explore the psychology that shapes Independent political identity.

The Psychological Forces Shaping Independents

Social identity theory examines how an individual’s self-concept is shaped by membership or non-membership in social groups. An independent political identity represents a distinct orientation toward politics and engagement in the United States. Political socialization in the United States occurs primarily through educational institutions, media exposure, and civic participation. The development of a political identity often precedes the formation of partisan attachments. Individuals can become engaged in politics without simultaneously identifying with either major party. One of the outcomes of teaching critical thinking in schools and universities is a more independent-minded electorate.

Individuals who declare themselves politically independent are motivated by a desire for more authentic forms of political engagement, rather than by the belief or expectation that they will adopt the political attitudes and patterns of behavior most associated with members of a particular party. Independents tend to value open dialogue more than party-affiliated citizens do; policy-oriented rather than candidate-based engagement more than partisans do; and attention to positions on specific issues more than partisans typically do.

Political independents are also more likely to voice skepticism concerning the credibility and relevance of information bearing organized party labels than are partisans. Independents view political parties as increasingly responsible for the imperfections and failings of the political system. All of these forces are converging to foster independent political identity in the United States.

Consequences of Growing Independent Identity

The increase in independent political identities has significant implications for the basic functioning of American democracy. And the legacy parties need to decide how they want to engage Independents moving forward. Consider what happens when a large portion of the electorate loses trust in the institutions of democracy or what happens when a large portion of the electorate declines to vote. The decline in trust and voter turnout is a reflection of the legacy parties focusing more and more on primary voters and less and less on general public engagement. This can be remedied by reducing the rigidity and demand for conformity within legacy parties.

Ultimately, the future of American democracy depends on the engagement of Independents as themselves, not by convincing them to join legacy parties. Similarly, independent political identity does not necessitate a singular new third political party, because independent political identity is not singular. A rise in independent political identity in the United States gives us the opportunity to reimagine a trustworthy, consensus-driven democracy that is not controlled by a two-party political system.

item.title: Self-Care for Caregivers of a Loved One in Health Decline
item.description:
Caregiving

Self-Care for Caregivers of a Loved One in Health Decline

How to sustain your own peace when caring for a loved one.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Caregiver burnout is real, and self-care is essential.
  • Reclaim a sense of peace and normalcy in your life during this painful time.
  • Self-care may include activities such as yoga, meditation, sound healing, or even walking in nature.
  • “It takes a village”: You need a team of supportive loved ones on whom to lean.
Source: LabRobotUIGear/Leonardo.AI

This is Part 3 of a series on loved ones in health decline. Read Part 1 and Part 2 here.

The adage “You can’t pour from an empty cup” seems trite and overused. However, when it comes to caregiver burnout, it has never been truer. If you have a loved one (including a family member or friend) in severe health decline, you know the feeling of burnout. While you may feel physical exhaustion, it’s often the emotional exhaustion that becomes overwhelming. It’s not selfish to take care of yourself during this very trying time in your life. It’s merely being true to yourself. In fact, taking care of yourself also includes surrendering control of the situation at times. Yet many in this position feel that self-care is not allowed and is even self-centered. Nothing could be further from the truth. But if you still feel that way, remind yourself that you cannot take care of your loved one if you are completely exhausted and burned out.

Compassion Fatigue When Caring for a Loved One

Compassion fatigue, most often associated with the helping professions (such as counselors and nurses), means taking on the emotional burden of others in poor health to the point where it’s detrimental to self. Setting emotional and physical boundaries is essential in these professions, and this entails maintaining a delicate balance of empathy and emotional self-care.

When you're caring for a loved one in severe health decline, compassion fatigue may be even more complicated. Because of the familial bond (or friendship bond) between yourself and the ill loved one, it’s much more challenging, and in some cases not realistic, to merely go home and forget about the loved one or family member. Indeed, the family member may even be living with the caregiver.

Whether or not you live with the declining loved one, though, the emotional tie still exists, and it remains with you even when you’re away from the loved one. Thus, burnout is even more of a possibility. There needs to be a team of caregivers, and self-care is essential.

Putting on Your Own Oxygen Mask First

Because of the emotional nature of caregiving for a loved one, self-care is your oxygen. Just as when a plane rapidly loses altitude, you need to put on your own oxygen mask first. Only then can you place a mask on your loved one and help them.

Source: Alejandro Quinones/Pexels

Self-Care Tips

You know yourself better than anyone else, so you probably know the best forms of your own self-care. However, there may be a few essential self-care tips that you haven’t considered. One of the most important go-to tips for self-care may be crying. Crying is an important release when a burden feels overwhelming, like there’s nowhere for the pain and emotional weight to go. There may even be physiological reasons for improved mood from this self-soothing activity. Crying is a healthy release for a mash-up of complex emotions you may be feeling, such as grief, resentment, guilt, and mixed feelings regarding the loved one’s decline.

Next up on the self-care list is journaling or free-form writing to express your feelings. Journaling can also help with the necessary emotional processing, including releasing the pain through crying. There may be feelings that you don’t feel comfortable expressing to others, and journaling is extremely helpful in releasing and processing these emotions.

Reach Out!

Leaning on trusted loved ones is essential for support when caregiving. They don’t need to have all the answers. In fact, it’s often best if they merely provide a supportive shoulder on which to lean (or a hug) rather than giving advice.

Of course, getting support and help from a qualified therapist or counselor can be an important step for many to navigate this situation and process the feelings. Individual counseling to process complex feelings, as well as group counseling and/or self-help groups, will help you to accept and normalize the many complex emotions you may be experiencing.

Avoiding Burnout: It Takes a Village

Remember you are not in this alone, in taking care of your loved one and in taking care of yourself. It takes a community, a village. Reach out to other trusted loved ones, a support group, and/or a counselor to help in your own vital self-care.

I cannot stress this enough: Do not burn yourself out! Caregiver burnout is quite real and can have serious physical and/or emotional well-being consequences when it is not addressed. Whether it involves emotional caretaking, physical caretaking, or both, keep in mind that caretaking is a marathon and not a sprint. Spread the burden and responsibility of care onto a community of helpers—a caregiving team—and get a professional paid caregiver to help whenever possible.

For the Mind, Body, and Spirit

Physical release can also be especially helpful for the caregiver. The self-healing practices of physical exercise and getting out in nature can calm the body and provide a sense of peace.

A calming and relaxing practice such as yoga, deep breathing, sound healing, or meditation may be just what you need at this challenging time in your life, and you may find that it soothes your soul. It may calm the “monkey mind” of thoughts zooming through your head and provide a much-needed oasis of peace and rest.

The Role of Spiritual Beliefs

Many people find that their spiritual or religious beliefs help them in traveling this journey. Believing in a power greater than ourselves may provide comfort for a situation in which we may struggle to find meaning.

Releasing the Burden (Even Temporarily) and Staying Engaged in Life

Stay engaged in your life. Feelings of overwhelm may make it feel safer to isolate. While alone time and emotional processing time are vital during this process, staying engaged in one’s life can also provide essential feelings of normalcy and stability. Getting out of the house, going for a walk in nature, or even going to a quiet café may provide the sense of normalcy and peace that are essential to soothing an overwhelmed caregiving soul.

Remember: Put on your oxygen mask first so you can help others!

item.title: Can AI Ease the Mental Load of Disaster Recovery?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can AI Ease the Mental Load of Disaster Recovery?

Responsible technology may help survivors preserve bandwidth and reclaim agency.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Disaster recovery demands the same mental capacities that chronic stress can impair.
  • Research with wildfire survivors shows that long-term recovery can become a “second full-time job.”
  • Survivors often need help acting on information, not simply more information. AI may ease survivor burden.
  • Responsible AI should expand access to support, prioritize safety, and strengthen human connection.

After wildfires repeatedly tore through my community in Northern California, I learned that surviving a disaster and recovering from one are two very different things.

The flames eventually go out. Then comes a second disaster: insurance negotiations, temporary housing, rebuilding decisions, financial calculations, endless forms, assistance deadlines, school disruptions, health concerns, and nonstop phone calls and emails.

Life keeps moving while you are trying to figure out how to put yours back together.

Phases of Disaster Recovery
Source: SAMHSA.gov

As a psychologist, I understood climate trauma intellectually. Living alongside disaster recovery taught me something else. Recovery itself requires an enormous amount of cognitive and emotional capacity. It demands attention, memory, planning, persistence, emotional regulation, and the ability to make consequential decisions and tolerate uncertainty, for months or years.

Yet chronic stress can disrupt those capacities. In my community, we came to call it “fire-brain”: the experience of staring at a relatively simple task and feeling as though your mind simply cannot get traction. Research increasingly supports what survivors have described for years: Disaster-related stress can interfere with executive functioning (Nan et al., 2025).

This creates a cruel mismatch. At precisely the moment people are depleted by loss, grief, displacement, financial strain, and disrupted routines, we ask them to become expert case managers for their own catastrophe. And as climate-related disasters become more frequent and more people enter long, complicated recoveries, that mismatch becomes increasingly urgent.

When we talk about climate adaptation, we tend to focus on physical infrastructure: stronger buildings, safer electrical grids, better evacuation routes. All of that matters. But there is another form of infrastructure we rarely name: human psychological capacity. We cannot seriously talk about adapting to a changing climate without asking how we help people preserve enough cognitive and emotional bandwidth to navigate what comes next.

When Recovery Becomes a Second Full-Time Job

In a recent study, The After Collective and Stanford collaborators surveyed and interviewed 115 people directly affected by the 2025 Eaton and Palisades wildfires in Los Angeles. More than a year after the fires, 67 percent were still displaced. Nearly three-quarters identified emotional or mental-health stress as one of their greatest recovery challenges, while 61 percent cited insurance and rebuilding paperwork and 52 percent cited financial strain among their biggest obstacles.

The numbers are sobering, but the stories underneath them were even more revealing. Survivors repeatedly described recovery as a “second full-time job” that adds an enormous mental load. They were trying to negotiate insurance claims, find housing, rebuild homes, parent children, return to work, manage finances, and make sense of changing programs and deadlines—all while simultaneously carrying grief and trauma.

The logistical and psychological challenges were not separate problems. They fed each other.

A confusing insurance process created more stress, which made it harder to concentrate on the insurance process. Financial uncertainty disrupted sleep, making consequential decisions harder. Small administrative demands became overwhelming when layered onto everything else a family had already lost.

Many were already drowning in information. But information and capacity to act are not the same thing. They wanted help figuring out what applied to them, what mattered now, what could wait, and how to get the next difficult thing done.

If part of the challenge of disaster recovery is that our systems demand more cognitive and emotional capacity than survivors have available, then we should be asking a different question: How might we design support that gives some of that capacity back?

Where Might Technology Help?

A machine cannot understand the human experience of loss, but it may be able to shoulder some of the work that consumes scarce survivor bandwidth.

Some recovery tasks are well suited to technology: sorting multiple information streams, translating jargon and instructions, identifying relevant resources, and breaking overwhelming processes into manageable next steps. Used well, these tools could provide cognitive scaffolding, helping people conserve attention and energy for the decisions and activities that truly require human judgment.

Recovery is more than an information problem. It is an emotional one, too.

A person staring at an insurance denial at 1 a.m. may not need more information first. They may need help slowing down, getting grounded, identifying the next manageable step, and knowing where to turn for human support.

There may be a responsible role for technology here, but not as a replacement for therapists, case managers, neighbors, or community. It may instead provide the psychological scaffolding for recovery: setting realistic expectations, offering evidence-informed coping tools, helping break problems into smaller steps, and generating pathways to people who can assist.

The goal is to preserve agency. At its best, responsible technology could help a disaster survivor in distress understand, regulate, act, and connect to a real human.

What Responsible AI for Disaster Recovery Requires

Possibility is not the same as responsibility. If disaster survivors are going to use AI-enabled tools while displaced, grieving, overwhelmed, and making consequential decisions, we should set a high bar for what they are designed to do and, more importantly, not do.

Responsible technology in disaster recovery should:

  • Reduce burden, not accelerate dysfunction. Technology should make complicated systems easier to navigate, not simply optimize systems that are already failing people.
  • Expand the safety net. Ethical AI should mobilize its benefits for the people and communities most vulnerable to climate disruption so that new technology narrows inequality rather than deepening it.
  • Connect people to people. AI cannot care about us, but responsibly designed tools can strengthen pathways to peers, community organizations, clinicians, and other trusted human support. The goal should be timely support, not continuous companionship.
  • Earn trust. Protect privacy, be transparent about limitations, and prioritize accurate, locally relevant information. Adoption will only move at the speed of trust.

AI will not fix fragmented recovery systems, replace the power of community, or solve the climate crisis. Even more importantly, if we are building AI in the name of climate adaptation, we also have to reckon with its environmental footprint, including the energy, water, and infrastructure required to power it. But perhaps one worthy use is helping people in distress preserve enough psychological capacity to take the next step and reclaim some agency over what comes next.

item.title: Bet on Your Friends
item.description:
Friends

Bet on Your Friends

What game nights teach men that betting apps can't.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Game nights are great ways to make and keep friends.
  • Game nights are more about ritual than who wins.
  • Make room at the table for others to play as well.
Pull up a chair!
Source: Mart Production / Pexels

I'm not much of a gambler. I tell people I gamble on startups and the stock market.

In high school, my friends and I played a lot of board games and cards. Mostly it was an excuse to drink cheap Black Label beer and smoke Camel Lights until well past 2 a.m. I was never any good at most of the games. We never played for money, only for shots of Jägermeister for the losers. Yeah, that stuff was big in the '80s.

It didn't matter who won. What mattered was that we were all at the table together.

Not much has changed. These days I play cards with family, and we put up some money, counted in quarters, for whoever wins at the end. I've been in a couple of fantasy leagues, but they never grabbed me. Mine were online, and I never got any sense of brotherhood from a screen.

Sports betting apps have made gambling easier than ever, and for a lot of men that's a real problem. But the problem isn't the bet. It's betting alone.

Why Apps Can't Replace the Table

The American Institute for Boys and Men has been tracking what happened when sports betting moved onto our phones. In a recent policy brief, its researchers point out that in just eight years, legal sports betting went from a niche activity in Nevada to a mass-market product on every smartphone. Today, nearly all bets are placed online.

What drove that growth? Frictionless apps, built on the same playbook as social media: Remove every obstacle, reward you at random, and ping you to come back.

Game night runs on friction. Somebody has to find a night that works, clear the kitchen table, and bring the drinks. Somebody has to settle whether it’s quarters or bragging rights. That hassle keeps most people from playing too often. An app has none of it. It’s open anytime, anywhere, and it doesn’t care if anyone else shows up.

That friction is the whole point. It turns a game into a ritual. Every one of those small jobs is a reason to show up for each other.

The app keeps the game and removes the gathering. You still get the rush of winning and the sting of losing. You just get them alone, on your couch, at 1 a.m.

That’s not a game night. That’s a habit. And for some men, it becomes something worse.

The Table Takes Care of Its Own

My family game nights are about playing and being together. We do bet, but the pool is usually a jar of quarters that anyone can draw from. It’s more about bragging rights than how much you win. The stakes are there to make losing sting a little without breaking the bank.

That jar is the whole idea. Nobody gets priced out of the game.

Turns out that’s not just my table. A recent study of Swedish poker players found the men capped buy-ins and rebuys because they were worried about each other’s money. The care kept the competition in check. The apps work the other way. Sportsbooks have all the data they need to spot a bettor who’s spiraling. Without regulation, the AIBM brief warns, that same data can be used to keep him betting. And the business depends on it: At one major U.S. sportsbook, half a percent of customers generated more than 70 percent of the revenue.

Think about that. At the table, your friends notice when you’re in too deep. The app notices too. It just wants something different.

Your friends watch out for you. The app watches you.

Every Group Needs a Game

Take the money out completely and the table still works.

Rage Against the Machine guitarist Tom Morello plays Dungeons & Dragons in actor Joe Manganiello's basement. Most of the group played as kids, took decades off for careers and families, then came back.

Morello compares it to a high-stakes poker game, except nobody is betting anything. He calls it "a game where friends gather that's taken deadly seriously." The seriousness comes from the friends, not the stakes.

The group has rules, too. When Morello wanted to bring in a dad from his kid's carpool, Manganiello almost said no. He wanted to keep the group tight. The new guy turned out to be Game of Thrones co-creator D.B. Weiss. He got in, then got called out for texting at the table. Every lasting group has unwritten rules like that.

Screenwriters John August and Craig Mazin have kept a D&D campaign going for years. When the pandemic hit, they moved it online rather than drop it.

That's what a game gives men. Something to do with your hands, so the talking happens side-by-side. A learning curve, so joining means something. And a reason to come back, so the group doesn't drift. It's a core idea in The Male Friendship Experience: Friendship needs structure, or it fades.

Pull Up a Chair

You don't need a celebrity basement or a jar of quarters. You need a table, a game, and a few guys willing to show up.

A recent Psychology Today piece, "Making Friends as We Age," makes the case that friendship often comes down to logistics: the same people showing up at the same place and time. Card games are one of the ways people are making that happen.

Here's how to start:

  • Pick a game with a little complexity: cards, dominoes, a board game, etc. There should be something to learn.
  • Keep the stakes low: quarters, bragging rights, or nothing at all.
  • Set a rhythm, not a rigid schedule. Once a month is plenty.
  • Put the phones away. The texting rule applies to everyone.
  • Invite one guy who doesn't know how to play. Then teach him.

That last one matters most. Somebody once taught you the game. Somebody made room for you at the table. Now it's your turn. Pay it forward. Play for both the love of the game and for the brotherhood it creates.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Disrespect
item.description:
Leadership

The Hidden Cost of Disrespect

Our chosen words shape trust and opportunities long after the conversation ends.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Respect influences relationships, goodwill, trust, and future opportunities.
  • Genuine respect allows us to disagree without diminishing another person’s dignity.
  • Reliable Respect is demonstrated through consistency, particularly when agreement may be difficult to reach.
Source: patricksommer / Pixabay

About 20 of us sat at tables arranged in a large rectangle in the hospital conference room. The configuration was intended to encourage dialogue. At one end sat five senior executives representing academic, clinical, and hospital leadership. Around the remaining “U” of the rectangle sat surgeons, some of us dressed in suits and others still in scrubs after coming directly from their operating rooms.

The purpose of the meeting was to discuss a proposed partnership that had raised several concerns within our department. As one of the spokespersons for my colleagues, I expressed our concerns, including the potential negative implications for patient care and the institution's reputation.

As the discussion progressed, the tension in the room became palpable, and before I could finish, a silver-haired executive interrupted. "That is the stupidest thing I've ever heard. You know nothing about business."

The room fell silent.

This was the first time we had met. He knew nothing of my background or experience, not that it should have mattered. Taken aback by his comment, I instinctively paused before responding. "It's good to know how you feel. Again, this is our position."

The following day, another senior executive who had attended the meeting approached me. He expressed appreciation for how I had handled the exchange and apologized on behalf of his colleague.

One Moment, Two Responses

I have often reflected on that moment. Two executives representing the same leadership team had responded very differently to the same disagreement. One had dismissed a perspective without appearing willing to consider it. The other recognized the impact of that reaction and took the initiative to acknowledge it.

Neither had changed the underlying disagreement, yet each had influenced how I felt about working with them in the future.

What Respect Makes Possible

In my previous Psychology Today post, I described respect as the emotional currency of success. This experience offers an example of what I meant.

I remained willing to work professionally with both executives. Our responsibilities to the institution and, ultimately, to our patients had not changed. However, my willingness to extend myself beyond those responsibilities had. I was less inclined to offer additional support to the executive who had dismissed our concerns and more inclined to support the one who had acknowledged what happened. Neither executive had asked anything further of me, yet their responses had already influenced the possibilities for future collaboration.

We often think about respect in terms of relationships—how people treat us, whether we feel valued, and the quality of our interactions—but respect also influences our goodwill, the opportunities we extend, and the trust we place in others. These consequences are not always immediately visible. They accumulate through interactions and the emotional imprints they leave in us, sometimes long after the words themselves have been forgotten.

Beyond Politeness and Agreement

Respect did not require me to abandon my position, nor did it require the executive to agree with it. It required a willingness to consider another perspective without diminishing the person expressing it.

This is where I believe genuine respect differs from performative politeness or agreeableness. We can choose courteous words or signal agreement while remaining unwilling to consider another person's perspective. We can also disagree firmly while demonstrating that their contribution has been heard and taken seriously. That distinction matters in families, workplaces, communities, and institutions where people with different responsibilities and experiences must find ways to work together.

We all bring assumptions into our interactions. Our experiences, beliefs, and expectations often influence how we interpret what others say. The opportunity lies in remaining curious about what each brings to the discussion, rather than drawing conclusions based on incomplete information.

The Respect We Choose to Practise

Over the years, I've found myself returning to my simple framework for managing stress in a challenging moment while remaining grounded in respect: the 3Rs (Reflect, Reframe, Respond).

Reflection creates an opportunity to recognize what we are feeling and the assumptions influencing our interpretation. Reframing allows us to consider what else might be true through curiosity and asking questions. Responding is where we choose how to act, ideally in a way that reflects both our values and the circumstances before us, which sometimes means choosing not to engage further.

These steps are not always deliberate or perfectly executed. What matters is the repeated effort to create space between what we experience and what we choose to do next.

Treating others with respect for their inherent dignity does not mean accepting harmful behaviour, avoiding accountability, or extending unlimited goodwill. We can fulfil our obligations while recognizing that trust and the willingness to offer additional support are influenced by how people conduct themselves.

This is particularly important in leadership, where the effects of an interaction often extend well beyond the individuals directly involved. How we respond can influence not only the person before us, but also those who witness the exchange.

The Influence We May Never See

We rarely know all the opportunities that arise because someone trusts us, appreciates our contribution, or remembers how we treated them during a conversation. Nor do we necessarily know which opportunities never materialize because an interaction diminished that trust. The executive who approached me the following day may not have realized how much his acknowledgment mattered. His colleague may never have known how his words influenced my perception of his credibility as a leader. Both left an impression.

Leadership is not limited to formal authority. Each of us influences others through the assumptions we bring, the perspectives we carry, and the way we respond when our views are challenged. What I call Reliable Respect is reflected in the consistency of those choices, particularly when circumstances make respect difficult to demonstrate. It allows others to trust that their perspectives will be considered, even when agreement is challenging.

If respect is the emotional currency of success, its value is reflected not simply in the courtesy we extend, but in the understanding, trust, and goodwill our interactions make possible. Sometimes, we only discover that value in what happens next.

item.title: Beyond 'Make This Go Away': Kids and Mental Health
item.description:
Parenting

Beyond 'Make This Go Away': Kids and Mental Health

Seven things you want your child to know about navigating their emotional life.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Kids get stuck when they are overwhelmed and feel like there is nothing they can do to help.
  • Parents want to help kids feel better, but deeper than rescue or fixing is helping kids understand themselves.
  • Kids can learn to become interpreters of their thoughts and feelings rather than seeing them as facts.
  • They can learn to zoom in to identify thoughts that come up, then zoom out and "fact-check" the thoughts.
Kids need our help navigating their emotional life.
Source: IONs/iStock

“She has no idea how to navigate this.” “He is so overwhelmed, he doesn’t know how to navigate this.” Whether we are talking about kids who are wired to feel things more intensely, or any child caught in a tough moment, often the first place kids land with their emotions is confusion and discomfort. And hey, isn’t that where we all land first? But here’s what happens next for kids: They feel like there is nothing they can do but wait until the feeling goes away. They turn to us in their distress with the unspoken request: “Make this go away.”

And of course, as parents, we want our kids to feel better, and we can and we should. But there’s a deeper way to do that than distracting or fixing things, and that is: helping our kids understand themselves better.

Toward Is Forward: We Have to Go There With Our Kids So They Can Learn the Way

Our most fundamental direction as parents: Toward is forward. Rather than steering our kids away from whatever they are feeling with distraction or avoidance, paradoxically, we can teach them that finding out more about what sets them off in the first place by thinking about the story their thoughts are telling them about it is the best way to feel better. When you see feelings as information to be interpreted, not facts to be followed, kids feel empowered to edit their thoughts, seek other perspectives, and choose the best ones. Increasingly, they learn to take with them from experiences only what is most helpful and true, and leave behind automatic distortions and maladaptive beliefs.

By teaching kids to turn inward and learn to use their thoughts to understand and make sense of what happens in their life, we show them the paths through that help them to feel in charge and to end up in a better place than they started. We can help kids move from “this is too much” to “I can figure it out.”

This is the essence of preventive mental health.

There are so many landmarks and pathways to help kids find their way through their emotional life. Here are seven starters that will help orient kids to getting the lay of the land so they can feel more confident about how to help themselves.

  1. Good mental health is about navigating feelings, not not having uncomfortable ones. Feelings are normal. “Good mental health” isn’t the absence of uncomfortable feelings; it’s knowing how to navigate when they come up. Rather than thinking: “What’s wrong with me? Why am I feeling this way?” Kids need to know there are no “wrong” landing places. Wherever they’ve landed is an opportunity to find out important messages from within and decide what they mean.
  2. See your child as separate from their thoughts: Build agency, not identity. We can help kids not confuse themselves with their feelings by doing the separation ourselves: Rather than going in the direction of “why are you thinking that?” ask instead: “That’s a powerful thought—what do you think about that? You are the final word on your thoughts.” We are giving them agency in our conversations with them, which they will then carry and internalize—"I should check in with myself and see what I think about this." Best sentence starters for parents—"I wonder if…” or “I wonder what…” “I’m having a different idea, but I want to hear yours first…” Sharing the job is how you help kids turn inward and trust what they find.
  3. Feelings come in two parts: the part we need to sit with—how it feels—and then the part we have to solve for—what it needs. It’s kind of like a seesaw we need to balance between feeling and doing something because we need both. Honor the feelings, and when you toggle to the other side—what needs to be done—it doesn’t mean that the feelings don’t matter, it’s that you and your growth matter more. When parents understand this, they won’t rush their child through their feelings, and kids won’t feel like their parents “don’t get it” or just want to “fix it.”
  4. Thoughts and feelings are first-draft signals that we interpret. Feelings come with messages. For example, when someone hurts our feelings: They are so mean! No one likes me! They are first drafts, and the first is the worst. We want to know what is hiding under the feeling. We get specific, or what’s called granular, to find out: What exactly is the thought? Then we can zoom out and spin around the idea, look at it from different angles, get different perspectives or opinions, and decide which “opinion” feels most true, most fair to ourselves, and most helpful. I call it “fact-checking,” and there are three easy ways to do it: Ask: What would I say to a friend in this situation? What would a friend say to me? What would a trusted wise guide—your inner board of directors—advise? Importantly, getting other opinions doesn’t mean your child’s view is “wrong.” It’s about getting in the habit of broadening the view to see what else could be true.
  5. Is a thought important or just stuck? Just because something is important doesn’t mean you have to think about it all the time. Is it important, or just stuck? Feelings change! You can tell yourself: This is how I am feeling now, and that’s OK. I’ll check in later and see how I feel. Help your child ask themselves: Is it necessary and helpful to think of this now? (Usually not!) Compartmentalization is an important skill. You can suggest your child “make an appointment” to spend 5 or 10 minutes thinking about a topic and fact-checking it, and if the thought comes up at other times, your child can learn to say: “Not now, I’m busy!”
  6. Everyone has things that are hard for them; we make progress step by step. Kids get frozen when trying something new because they feel like they have to do everything perfectly, and it’s (rightfully) too hard. That’s not how any of us grow. Instead, teach kids to visualize all the possible small steps between where they are now and where they want to be, then choose just the step they are ready for. Practice with dry runs at home.
  7. We are wired to see what’s wrong. Practice looking for the good on purpose. We know that helping kids feel good and find the good isn’t about telling them to be happy, or just be more positive. Join in with your child: The brain is wired to find problems, the weeds, and it can feel like everything is a weed. I suggest imagining what I call a “Some Magnet”—a magnet, or something like a metal detector, that we can run over our day and listen for the beep-beep-beep when it finds things that were nice or OK. Make it a family practice.

Children’s mental health is built in the back-and-forth of our conversations with them. Kids knowing that they can bring their emotional lives to us is more than a comfort. It is how they are going to learn the skills to make sense of their inner lives, with our support alongside them for the journey. Over time, kids internalize these ideas and light up a navigational route they can find themselves and carry on their own. What is one idea you hope your child knows about how emotions work?

item.title: Why We Crave Purpose
item.description:
Flow

Why We Crave Purpose

Finding your ikigai.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Ikigai is a Japanese idea that translates roughly to "the happiness of always being busy.”
  • Finding your ikigai is the key to a longer life because it represents the sweet spot of living.
  • Our most joyful and unforgettable times are typically the most productive times.

Ask yourself this central question: When were you genuinely the happiest in your life? If you are being totally honest, you might find that the most joyful and unforgettable times were your most productive ones.

Human beings are meaning-making machines—perpetual storytellers of the highest order. We are constantly weaving interpretation and texture into every aspect of our lives. Every day, we are organically compelled to justify our beliefs and actions, and for good reason; “meaning” gives us drive and determination to keep on going even when things get tough and we are running on empty. But why?

In an inherently disordered world, our brains operate like principal narrators—realizing cognitive designs out of unpredictability and transforming experience into historied structure. But this isn’t an esoteric coincidence; it is a mental survival device. It’s one of the most essential parts of being human. We can’t stop doing it, and we shouldn’t.

If we stray from the focused states of the mind that keep us connected to our daily purpose, we may decompensate and fall apart. For example, imagine if every person in the world were stripped of their daily purpose for an extended period—like work, school, taking care of children, keeping house, doing laundry. In time, there could be global pandemonium. This loss of purpose and structure might create an existential crisis of high anxiety. Many individuals would begin obsessing and worrying about all the wrong things. Idle time for the human mind is worse than the devil’s playground; it’s the devil’s penitentiary.

Order and structure help us find purpose and meaning on a daily basis, and we need resolution to function well. Our life’s purpose and the responsibilities of each day, no matter how mundane, help us survive. They prevent us from negatively overthinking our ephemeral existence.

Consequently, while acquiring awareness and deeply analyzing our lives is important, we don’t want to over-dwell on it either. If we don’t have focus on immediacy in our lives, we tend to look backward more often too, sometimes with regret. We obsess about mistakes and bad choices with more scrutiny. The despair is liable to creep in and make us dissect the past when we have no business doing so.

What Is Ikigai?

Ikigai is a Japanese idea that translates roughly to "the happiness of always being busy.” Finding your Ikigai is the key to a longer life because it represents the sweet spot of living. Ikigai encompasses the small daily joys, meaningful relationships, and personal fulfillment that make waking up each morning worthwhile. That’s why Japanese people never really retire from the workforce or from their personal responsibilities that give them resolve.

From the international bestseller, Ikigai: The Japanese Secret to a Long Happy Life, Hector Garcia and Francesc Miralles tell us, “We have to focus on increasing the time we spend on activities that bring us to a state of flow, rather than allowing ourselves to get caught up in activities that offer immediate pleasure – like eating too much, abusing drugs or alcohol, or stuffing ourselves with chocolate in front of the TV.”

The Power of Flow States

Everyone has in some way experienced “flow” states that are remarkable. Flow states are sometimes enjoyable, sometimes obsessive periods of time when you are so absorbed in what you are doing that you don’t realize the passing of time. Professional athletes often speak of being “in the zone” when they are performing at their highest level because they are free of any distraction or doubt. They are fearless, determined, and locked in.

For the most part, people define flow states as happy recesses of time. “Flow delight” can also be wishes, aspirations, or daydreams. It can be an imaginary scenario of being generous, courageous, or magnanimous. It can be contemplating ourselves seeking higher education, buying our first house, starting a business, even falling in love. Whatever you aspire to, and the time you spend dreaming about it, is a variant of flow. In other words, if flow begets purpose and vice versa, it’s a winning combo because we can be better, tougher, wiser, by simply exposing ourselves to a schematic of intention.

Flow states can be productive in other ways too. As mentioned, they can be born from intervals of intensity where you are so fixated on an important task, a project, an assignment, or even a cause, that it occupies your mind in an industrious way. The downside is, they can feel excessively emotional, impassioned, and urgent too. However, that's usually a sign that your inner superpower is activated and perhaps the greater good is being prioritized. The creative need to protect, safeguard, improve, and be a support to someone or something is its own unique process of flow.

So, whether it’s a happy and enjoyable flow state, or an intensely focused one, or any kind of daily routine or ritual, exalting it as a gift and seeing it as being at your best is vital for creating meaningful intent. Do not take it for granted. Find your everyday purpose, your “flow,” whatever that might be. Honor it, respect it, and stick to it. According to ikigai philosophy, you might live longer too.

Albert Einstein famously said, “A happy man is too satisfied with the present to dwell on the future.”
